analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or raising premiums based on a person's genetic information.
analysis.headline: Despite 76 cosponsors, the bill never got a vote in any House committee or on the floor, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for health insurers to deny or cancel coverage, or to change premiums and terms, based on someone's genetic information or their use of genetic testing [S2][S3]. It also barred insurers from demanding genetic information from applicants and from sharing it without written permission [S3]. It was introduced in December 1995, sent to two House committees, and never received a single vote before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People with a family history or genetic test result showing elevated risk for disease. Without protection, they could be denied coverage, charged more, or afraid to take a genetic test because the result could follow them to their insurer.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insurers from denying or canceling coverage, or varying premiums and terms, based on genetic information or on having requested genetic services [S2][S3].
Bars insurers from requesting or requiring anyone to disclose genetic information about themselves or family members [S3].
Blocks insurers from disclosing genetic information without prior written authorization, renewed for each disclosure [S3].
Gives individuals a private right of action, including injunctions and monetary damages, enforceable in state and federal courts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would lose the ability to use genetic information in underwriting, which their industry argued would make pricing less precise. The cost of covering higher-risk people would be spread across premiums generally.

drawbacks.text: Barring use of genetic information removes one tool insurers use to price risk, which insurers argue can push premiums up for everyone or encourage people to buy coverage only after learning their risk [S3].
The bill does not require any plan to cover particular benefits, so even a protected person could still face limited coverage [S3].
Enforcement for employer plans runs through the Secretary of Labor under existing ERISA procedures, a mechanism critics of ERISA enforcement have long called weak [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection addresses a real and growing fear as genetic testing spread: that a test result could cost you your insurance. The honest trade-off is that forbidding insurers from pricing genetic risk shifts some cost into general premiums. On balance, the protection is the kind most people cannot buy for themselves individually, which is why it later became law in broader form.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees and three subcommittees, where it sat without any markup or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced December 7, 1995, by Rep. Louise Slaughter with 24 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
Referred to the Commerce Committee and the Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee, then in late December to three subcommittees [S5].
No committee markup, report, or floor vote ever occurred; the last recorded action was the sponsor's introductory remarks in March 1996 [S5].
It attracted 76 cosponsors, including 5 Republicans and 2 independents, before dying at the end of the 104th Congress [S4].
Congress addressed genetic discrimination in health insurance more narrowly in the 1996 portability law, and a comprehensive genetic nondiscrimination law (GINA) was not enacted until 2008.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the ability to use genetic information in underwriting, and people at genetic risk of disease stayed exposed to being charged more or denied coverage.

for.name: Rep. Louise McIntosh Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor in introductory remarks [S1][S5].

for.name: 5 of 230 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Constance Morella, who was an original cosponsor [S3][S4].

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral, chaired by Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup during the 104th Congress [S5].

against.name: House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on employer-employee relations; no further action was taken [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was heavily Democratic — 69 of 76 cosponsors — but included 5 Republicans and 2 independents, and no vote ever occurred to test the split.

industries.note: The bill would have barred insurers from denying coverage, raising premiums, or demanding genetic information — ending a pricing tool their business relied on. Insurers' interest in keeping that tool ran directly against people's interest in keeping coverage after a genetic test [S2][S3].
By barring insurers from requiring or penalizing genetic information, the bill would have made people less afraid to get genetic tests or counseling, expanding demand for those services [S2][S3].
